teaching.causalExplanation: Here's how strongly each push tries to turn the nut, shown by a curved arrow. The right-angle push has the biggest turning effect. The thirty degree push has one only half as big. And the push along the handle just shoves on the nut, with no turning effect at all. The turning effect of a force about a pivot is called torque. Torque isn't a force. It's what a force does to rotation. So why does the same force give more torque at some angles than others? Start with the simplest case, the push at right angles. A longer spanner makes a stuck nut easier, and a door pushed near its hinge barely moves. Distance from the pivot matters. Push halfway along the handle, and you get only half the turning effect. For a force at right angles to the line from the pivot, the torque is the distance times the force. Tau equals r F. Here that's zero point two five metres times eighty newtons, twenty newton metres. Torque is measured in newton metres. It isn't energy, so we never write it in joules. Now the push at thirty degrees. Split it into two components. One runs along the handle. It just pulls on the nut through its centre, so it can't turn it. The other is at right angles to the handle, and only that part does the turning. It's F sin theta, where theta is the angle between the handle and the force. Eighty times sin thirty is forty newtons, so the torque is zero point two five times forty, ten newton metres. Half the force at right angles, so half the torque.

scenes.teachingReason: So what about the push straight along the handle? Its line of action passes right through the pivot, so the moment arm is zero, and so is the torque. That's why a door won't open if you push its edge straight towards the hinges.
